extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism researchers, journalism students, and practicing journalists interested in news values and tabloidization
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying criteria that define 'tabloidization' of mainstream news and contrasting those with broadsheet/news-quality values; useful for analyzing news content, newsroom practice, or platform effects. The page summarizes conceptual dimensions, a three-level model (selection, writing, presentation), drivers, and implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabloidization (general definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The shift toward tabloid-style news values in mainstream media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterized by moves such as personalization, sensationalism, trivialization, emotional framing, visual prominence, entertainment over information, less politics/more lifestyle, and shorter stories. Use this as an overarching descriptor when multiple tabloid-style features co-occur in coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Esser's 3-Level Model — News selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Level 1 of Esser's model: which stories are chosen to be covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether editorial selection privileges individualized, sensational, entertainment, celebrity, scandal, or visually rich events over public-policy, institutional, or complex social-issue stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Esser's 3-Level Model — News writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Level 2 of Esser's model: how stories are written and framed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate narrative techniques (personalization, emotional framing, brevity, drama), use of sources, depth of analysis, and whether writing privileges entertainment or shock over contextual information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Esser's 3-Level Model — News presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Level 3 of Esser's model: visual and format aspects of news delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look at headline style, imagery prominence, layout, multimedia emphasis, and other design/format choices that favor visual impact and quick consumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting events primarily through individuals rather than institutions or structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories foreground personal actors, anecdotes, and biographical details; scoring note — high personalization is a key tabloid marker and often reduces systemic/contextual explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasizing shocking, emotionally arousing elements of a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes attention-grabbing language, exaggerated claims, or selection of the most lurid details; anti-patterns include prioritizing shock over factual accuracy or proportionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trivialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Reducing complex issues to light, superficial coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage emphasizes trivial or entertainment aspects rather than substantive public-interest information; indicator of tabloid orientation when complex policy issues are simplified or sidelined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Framing stories to elicit emotions before or instead of conveying factual context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritizes feelings and personal reactions; may use quotes, imagery, or narrative structure designed to provoke sympathy, outrage, or amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual prominence / Visualization
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of strong images, visuals, and image-dominant layouts in news presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories chosen or framed for their photo/video potential; high visual prominence signals tabloid-style presentation and can overshadow textual explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entertainment over information
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritizing entertainment value rather than informational depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content choices, tone, and formats are driven by amusement or diversion. Measure by presence of quizzes, listicles, celebrity gossip, or light features where public-interest information would be expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Less politics, more lifestyle
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage shifts from political/institutional matters toward lifestyle, consumer, and everyday-interest content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track topic mix: decline in policy/institutional stories and rise in lifestyle, consumer, and leisure coverage indicates tabloidizing tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shorter stories / Brevity
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories are shorter and structured for quick consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of brief paragraphs, little background/context, and formats optimized for short attention spans; scoring — brevity coupled with low context is a tabloid marker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drama (narrative tension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructing reports as dramatic narratives with conflict and tension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes plot, villains/victims, and episodic tension; often reduces analytical nuance in favor of story arc and cliffhangers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebrity focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritizing stories about famous people and their private lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage emphasizes celebrity actions, scandals, and gossip; measure by share of celebrity-related items and prominence given to celebrity sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex / scandal
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclination to highlight sexual content, scandalous behavior, or moral transgression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection and framing emphasize scandalous details; such angles often drive click/attention but can distort public understanding of importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crime spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting crime coverage as spectacle with emphasis on sensational elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritizes dramatic elements of crime (violence, gore, lurid detail) and often foregrounds spectacle over systemic causes or policy implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports as entertainment dimension
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating sports coverage primarily as entertainment rather than social/cultural analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing sports stories for spectacle, hero narratives, and entertainment rather than structural critique or policy connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lifestyle / consumer content
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasis on consumer culture, lifestyle features, and practical tips for everyday living.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increase in how-to, shopping, fashion, food, and wellness pieces at the expense of civic reporting indicates tabloidizing orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local / parochial focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Concentrating on local, parochial stories with immediate local interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not inherently tabloid, an exclusive tilt toward parochialism combined with sensationalization and personalization is identified as a tabloid trait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-policy depth (broadsheet value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing in-depth coverage of public policy issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure by investigative reporting, policy analysis, and explanatory context; listed as a core broadsheet standard contrasted with tabloidization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional accountability (broadsheet value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Holding institutions accountable through reporting and scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes watchdog journalism, exposing institutional failures, and sustained scrutiny of public actors; low presence indicates tabloid drift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign affairs (broadsheet value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantive coverage of international affairs and global issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broadsheet orientation prioritizes foreign reporting and contextual international analysis rather than parochial or celebrity coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytical complexity (broadsheet value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing complex, nuanced analysis rather than simplified narratives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess depth of explanation, presence of multiple perspectives, and resistance to oversimplified frames.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-form investigations (broadsheet value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Carrying out long-form investigative journalism that uncovers systemic issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicator of resources and public-service ethos; decline signals cost-cutting and tabloidizing pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source diversity (broadsheet value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a diverse range of authoritative sources rather than a narrow set of voices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counts of source types (experts, documents, officials, affected persons) and avoidance of over-reliance on PR/celebrity sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue framing over personality (broadsheet value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Framing stories around issues, structures, and public consequences rather than personalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize systemic frames and policy impact; de-emphasize personalization and biographical emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical literacy in reporting (broadsheet value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of quantitative evidence, statistics, and numeracy in journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checks for correct use of numbers, context for statistics, and avoidance of misleading quantitative presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalizable (implicit newsworthiness criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories are judged newsworthy if they can be told through an individual's experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This implicit criterion favors selection of cases that personalize broader issues; overlaps with personalization but is framed as a newsworthiness test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualizable (implicit newsworthiness criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsworthiness is increased if the story has strong image or video potential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories with obvious photographic or video moments are favored for selection and placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brief (implicit newsworthiness criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for stories that can be communicated briefly and fit short attention spans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection and writing prioritize short-form items that require minimal background; indicator of tabloid-friendly format decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional hook (implicit newsworthiness criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that immediately elicit emotional responses are seen as more newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors favor items with clear emotional appeal (sympathy, outrage, amusement) often at the expense of balanced context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entertainment value (implicit newsworthiness criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A story's capacity to entertain increases its chance of selection and prominence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes humor, spectacle, or novelty; used to justify prominence even when civic importance is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebrity attached (implicit newsworthiness criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Association with a celebrity increases a story's perceived newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories with celebrity involvement are prioritized for placement and longer runtimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scandalous angle (implicit newsworthiness criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A scandalous or morally transgressive angle makes a story more likely to be selected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection favors details that suggest wrongdoing, impropriety, or dramatic fall from grace; can distort perception of prevalence/importance.
